lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Testing variables in a regression is harder. We ask whether each variable matters given all the others. <bookmark mark='b'/> The lasso selects variables but promises nothing about errors. <bookmark mark='c'/> Valid p-values for each variable are hard to get after selection, and impossible by classical means when p exceeds n. <bookmark mark='d'/> Rina Foygel Barber and Emmanuel Candès found a way, in 2015, to control the false discovery rate of a selection made by almost any method: knockoffs.
lines.spoken: Testing variables in a regression is harder. We ask whether each variable matters given all the others. The lasso selects variables but promises nothing about errors. Valid p-values for each variable are hard to get after selection, and impossible by classical means when p exceeds n. Rina Foygel Barber and Emmanuel Candès found a way, in 2015, to control the false discovery rate of a selection made by almost any method: knockoffs.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Construct a fake copy of every variable, a knockoff, with two properties. <bookmark mark='b'/> Swapping any set of variables with their knockoffs leaves the joint distribution of all of them unchanged: each knockoff relates to the other variables exactly as its original does. <bookmark mark='c'/> And the knockoffs are made without looking at the outcome, so they are independent of it given the real variables. <bookmark mark='d'/> Each knockoff is a perfect matched control: it looks like its original in every way, but is certainly null.
lines.spoken: Construct a fake copy of every variable, a knockoff, with two properties. Swapping any set of variables with their knockoffs leaves the joint distribution of all of them unchanged: each knockoff relates to the other variables exactly as its original does. And the knockoffs are made without looking at the outcome, so they are independent of it given the real variables. Each knockoff is a perfect matched control: it looks like its original in every way, but is certainly null.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> When the variables are multivariate normal with a known covariance, the model-X knockoffs of Candès, Yingying Fan, Lucas Janson and Jinchi Lv have a closed form: <bookmark mark='b'/> draw each knockoff row from a normal whose mean and covariance are set by sigma and a diagonal matrix D. <bookmark mark='c'/> The simplest choice makes D a multiple of the identity, as large as positive definiteness allows. <bookmark mark='d'/> The larger D, the less each knockoff resembles its original, and the easier it is to tell a real variable from its fake.
lines.spoken: When the variables are multivariate normal with a known covariance, the model-X knockoffs of Candès, Yingying Fan, Lucas Janson and Jinchi Lv have a closed form: draw each knockoff row from a normal whose mean and covariance are set by sigma and a diagonal matrix D. The simplest choice makes D a multiple of the identity, as large as positive definiteness allows. The larger D, the less each knockoff resembles its original, and the easier it is to tell a real variable from its fake.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The original knockoffs of 2015 were fixed-X: constructed from the observed design so that the knockoffs have the same correlations among themselves as the originals, and with the originals except on the diagonal. <bookmark mark='b'/> That version needs at least twice as many observations as variables and a linear model with Gaussian errors. <bookmark mark='c'/> Model-X knockoffs instead treat the rows of X as random with a known distribution, and allow any relationship between y and X. <bookmark mark='d'/> In practice the distribution of X is estimated, and often only its means and covariances are matched, an approximation whose robustness is an active research question.
lines.spoken: The original knockoffs of 2015 were fixed-X: constructed from the observed design so that the knockoffs have the same correlations among themselves as the originals, and with the originals except on the diagonal. That version needs at least twice as many observations as variables and a linear model with Gaussian errors. Model-X knockoffs instead treat the rows of X as random with a known distribution, and allow any relationship between y and X. In practice the distribution of X is estimated, and often only its means and covariances are matched, an approximation whose robustness is an active research question.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Now fit any model to the real variables and their knockoffs together, for example a lasso on two p columns. <bookmark mark='b'/> For each variable, W j is the size of its coefficient minus the size of its knockoff's. <bookmark mark='c'/> A large positive W means the real variable clearly beat its fake. <bookmark mark='d'/> Any statistic works, provided the statistic obeys the joint flip-sign property: swapping a subset flips exactly those W signs and leaves the others unchanged.
lines.spoken: Now fit any model to the real variables and their knockoffs together, for example a lasso on two p columns. For each variable, W j is the size of its coefficient minus the size of its knockoff's. A large positive W means the real variable clearly beat its fake. Any statistic works, provided the statistic obeys the joint flip-sign property: swapping a subset flips exactly those W signs and leaves the others unchanged.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The proof is a coin flip. For a null variable, swapping it with its knockoff changes nothing about the data's distribution but flips the sign of W. Conditional on all magnitudes and nonnull statistics, the nonzero null signs are independent fair coins. <bookmark mark='b'/> Hence the number of nulls with W above t is mirrored by the number of W's below minus t. <bookmark mark='c'/> That count, plus one, over the number selected, estimates the false discovery proportion. <bookmark mark='d'/> Choose the smallest nonzero observed absolute W where the estimate is below q, or select none if there is no such threshold, and the false discovery rate is at most q, exactly, in finite samples, with no p-values, for any n and p.
lines.spoken: The proof is a coin flip. For a null variable, swapping it with its knockoff changes nothing about the data's distribution but flips the sign of W. Conditional on all magnitudes and nonnull statistics, the nonzero null signs are independent fair coins. Hence the number of nulls with W above t is mirrored by the number of W's below minus t. That count, plus one, over the number selected, estimates the false discovery proportion. Choose the smallest nonzero observed absolute W where the estimate is below q, or select none if there is no such threshold, and the false discovery rate is at most q, exactly, in finite samples, with no p-values, for any n and p.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> A simulated regression: four hundred observations, a hundred and fifty correlated variables, twenty real effects. The sixty largest W statistics, in order of size. <bookmark mark='b'/> Real variables in green stand tall above zero. Null variables come in both signs, as the coin-flip argument says. <bookmark mark='c'/> The knockoff+ threshold at ten percent selects twenty-three variables, three of them false.
lines.spoken: A simulated regression: four hundred observations, a hundred and fifty correlated variables, twenty real effects. The sixty largest W statistics, in order of size. Real variables in green stand tall above zero. Null variables come in both signs, as the coin-flip argument says. The knockoff+ threshold at ten percent selects twenty-three variables, three of them false.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Over twenty simulated regressions: the cross-validated lasso finds every real variable, but sixty-two percent of what it selects is false, Part 32's lesson again. <bookmark mark='b'/> The estimated knockoff FDR is eight point two percent, with a one point seven percentage-point Monte Carlo standard error across only twenty studies <bookmark mark='c'/> and still find ninety-seven percent of the real variables.
lines.spoken: Over twenty simulated regressions: the cross-validated lasso finds every real variable, but sixty-two percent of what it selects is false, Part 32's lesson again. The estimated knockoff FDR is eight point two percent, with a one point seven percentage-point Monte Carlo standard error across only twenty studies and still find ninety-seven percent of the real variables.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The striking feature of model-X knockoffs is where the assumption sits: on the distribution of the variables, not on how the outcome depends on them. Any outcome model, any machine-learning method, can produce the W's. <bookmark mark='b'/> In genetics, where genotypes along a chromosome are modeled by fitted hidden Markov models, this has been used at genome scale. <bookmark mark='c'/> The price is that the distribution of X must be right. <bookmark mark='d'/> A different exchangeability assumption, across observations, powers conformal prediction, in Part 34.
lines.spoken: The striking feature of model-X knockoffs is where the assumption sits: on the distribution of the variables, not on how the outcome depends on them. Any outcome model, any machine-learning method, can produce the W's. In genetics, where genotypes along a chromosome are modeled by fitted hidden Markov models, this has been used at genome scale. The price is that the distribution of X must be right. A different exchangeability assumption, across observations, powers conformal prediction, in Part 34.
